candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials. They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster . The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA. It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there. (Image credit: SETI) Why it mattered The Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute. "The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," SETI wrote of the broadcast in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's." candidates.raw_excerpt: Iceye announced its next-generation satellite, designed to provide synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging in as fine as 11 centimeter resolution for sovereign nations, and 16 cm for commercial customers. This marks the fifth generation, Gen5, of Iceye’s SAR constellation. The satellites are designed to provide faster downlink than the previous generation, at up to 1 Gbps of downlink speed, compared to 700 Mbps in the previous version. The satellites are also designed to collect more images per pass than the previous version, with 18 images per acquisition, compared to 15 images in the previous acquisition. Iceye did not state when the first Gen5 satellites will launch, but said that it can deliver Gen5 satellites to customers within 12 months of deal signing. Iceye CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company updates its satellite generations approximately every 18 months, and issues new software releases each quarter. “Time to decision is everything in space-based intelligence, whether you’re tracking a vessel or responding to a flood. Gen5 shortens it at every step: sharper and more images per pass, and AI analysis that starts in orbit,” Modrzewski commented. The first satellites in Iceye’s previous generation, Gen4, were launched in March of 2025. In comparison, Gen4 offers resolution up to 16 cm and up to 700 Mbps data downlink with a steerable antenna. Iceye stated that the new generation will be fully compatible with the ground segment of previous versions, so existing customers can onboard Gen5 satellites without change. China launched its self-developed electronic ship log system on Monday, marking a key step in the digital transformation of basic shipping documents.

A ship's log is a legally required original record of a vessel's voyage and serves as a key basis for maritime investigations, accident tracing and liability determination.

The newly launched system replaces manual transcription with automatic recording. Through ship-to-shore data synchronization, vessel management shifts from checking paper logs to accessing digital data. Digital signatures and blockchain-based recordkeeping help ensure records are authentic and tamper-proof, providing reliable evidence for maritime supervision and port state control inspections.

The system has completed sea trials on four cargo ships. Functions including automatic collection of basic information and data transmission back to shore have operated stably during testing, with positive results.

candidates.title: SpaceX Catches Starship In Landing After Orbital Flight for First Time
candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX successfully caught the Starship vehicle when it returned from an orbital flight on Saturday, marking a major milestone for the rocket’s development. The catch was a historic moment for SpaceX, but the launch had an anomaly in the first portion of the flight and did not catch the Super Heavy booster — making a double-catch mission still elusive. The mission launched on Friday, Nov. 13 at 4:47 p.m. CST from Starbase, Texas and wrapped up with the catch a day later at 3:20 p.m. CST on Saturday. At the start of the mission, the Super Heavy booster and Starship separated from each other about 2 minutes and 30 seconds into the mission. SpaceX was planning to attempt a catch of the Super Heavy booster, but reported that the boostback burn ended early due to an anomaly. The booster was diverted to an offshore landing in the Gulf and was seen exploding while it splashed down. On the ship side, Starship successfully performed an orbital insertion burn, successfully reaching orbit for the second time after first hitting the milestone in September . Starship then spent more than 21 hours in orbit. During that time it deployed 26 satellites for the Starlink V3 broadband constellation. SpaceX made the determination to return Starship to Earth and attempt the catch, which previous Starship flights have not been able to do. During the landing, Starship relit a single Raptor engine and performed a deorbit burn, then lit three engines to descend into the landing tower chopstick arms to uproarious cheers from the SpaceX team as Starship returned to Earth “Can you believe it? Mechzilla has caught the Starship,” SpaceX launch broadcast host Dan Huot said. “We’ve been waiting to hear that for a long time. Look at her. Baby, she’s back.” SpaceX has caught the Super Heavy booster in three previous flights, but this was the first time it caught the Starship portion after an orbital flight. candidates.raw_excerpt: The United Launch Alliance’s eagerly awaited return-to-flight of the Vulcan rocket today did not go as planned. An anomaly 10 minutes after launch meant the 40 Amazon Leo satellites did not reach orbit. ULA is investigating what went wrong. It is the first total failure in ULA’s history. This was just the fifth launch of Vulcan since the first in January 2024 . That was a great success, but since then only one other launch, the third , went as planned. On flights two and four , in 2024 and 2026 respectively, nozzles on the Northrop Grumman Solid Rocket Boosters (SRBs) malfunctioned. Although Vulcan’s core stage compensated for the underperformance and delivered the payloads to their intended destinations, the U.S. Space Force has been hesitant to use Vulcan for its most precious satellites. Several launches have been shifted to SpaceX, although the intent is to reassign some SpaceX missions back to ULA to keep the number of launches per company the same. ULA has a large backlog of commercial satellite orders including many for Amazon’s satellite internet constellation Amazon Leo. Today was intended to demonstrate Vulcan is ready for both commercial and government payloads. Vulcan is replacing ULA’s Delta and Atlas V rockets. The final Delta IV launched in 2024 . Six Atlas Vs remain, but are under contract to Boeing for Starliner. Vulcan is ULA’s future. Today’s launch was originally scheduled for Friday, but scrubbed by a pump failure at Air Liquide’s gaseous nitrogen (GN2) plant. Rescheduled for yesterday, that was postponed due to a network communication issue between ground equipment and the launch vehicle. Today’s liftoff at 12:11 pm ET slipped to the end of the 29-minute window because of oscillations in a liquid hydrogen pressure relief valve. candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) Why it mattered When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later. "In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus." The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO. The Green Bank Telescope collapse left a mass of twisted debris behind. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions. candidates.raw_excerpt:
Italy's data protection agency on Saturday fined Meta Platforms 805 million euros (about $887 million) after finding that the company accessed Android users' photos and videos without their consent or notice.

Meta had access to Android users' ​photos and videos through a Facebook app feature that ​suggested content from users' personal galleries that they could post, the Italian Data Protection Authority said in a statement.

Meta has 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately, it said, adding that around 20 million Android users in Italy have been affected.

A Meta spokesperson said the company would appeal, strongly disagreeing with the authority's decision and calling the fine "disproportionate."

"This is a simple feature that helps people share photos and videos on Facebook. ​Users must grant permission on their device before the feature can operate, and ‌they can change that permission at any time in their settings," the spokesperson said in a statement.

The investigation, which began in 2025, did not cover the possible use of the content to train artificial intelligence models, a practice Meta denied, the authority said.

The authority also said it reserved the right to assess separately a new feature, launched in 2026, that allows content from users' galleries to be processed in the cloud.

The fine is equivalent to about 0.47% of the group's global revenue, ​the authority said.

candidates.raw_excerpt:
SpaceX's Starship spacecraft returned to its launch site on Saturday and was successfully caught by the launch tower's giant mechanical arms for the first time, marking a major milestone in the company's efforts to develop a fully reusable rocket system.

The giant rocket lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility in the US state of Texas on Friday afternoon. After more than 22 hours in space, it returned to the launch site on Saturday, completing Starship's 15th flight test and its longest mission to date.

The Starship spacecraft performed its orbital insertion burn and entered Earth's orbit. It later deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites.

After emerging from thick clouds over the Texas coast, the spacecraft reignited three engines, flipped into a vertical position and slowed its descent toward the launch tower. The mechanical arms then successfully caught the spacecraft.

The mission had originally aimed to catch both the Starship spacecraft and its Super Heavy booster during the same flight. However, following a technical issue after stage separation, the booster was diverted from its planned return to the launch site and splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico.

A major step toward full reusability

SpaceX's Starship spacecraft and Super Heavy rocket, collectively referred to as Starship, represent a fully reusable transportation system designed to carry both crew and cargo to Earth orbit, the moon, Mars and beyond.

candidates.title: SpaceX Successfully Catches Starship Upper Stage
candidates.raw_excerpt: The answer to life, the universe, and everything is 42. Turns out, it was also the answer to catching a Starship, too.  SpaceX made history on Saturday, recovering a Starship upper stage from orbit for the first time. The chopstick arms of the Mechazills launch tower plucked Ship 42 out of the air in Starbase, Texas at 4:20pm ET.  Flight 15 lifted off from Starbase at 5:47pm ET Friday, deploying its payload and completing 14 orbits before heading home. More than 22 hours after liftoff, Ship relit a single Raptor engine to exit orbit, then flew back toward the Texas coast. It made a final “swoosh” maneuver over the Gulf, broke through the clouds, and lit three Raptors for a landing flip and slow descent into the tower’s waiting arms. “We caught a Starship,” SpaceX Communications Manager Dan Huot said, ending the marathon 23-hour livestream. “And now everything changes.”  Catch 42: Catching the upper stage unlocks the next step toward full reusability for Starship. Now that Ship 42 came home intact, it could—in theory—fly again.  On SpaceX’s Q3 earnings call, CEO Elon Musk said the goal is to “immediately land the rocket and launch it again, just like an airplane.” He also said at the time that he expects to reach weekly Starship flights at some point in the first half of 2027. Ship 42 also carried a couple of Easter eggs, including “Don’t Panic” on the rocket—-nod to The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy—- and a heat-shield tile signed and installed by YouTuber MrBeast. The one that got away: Super Heavy Booster 22 never made it to the tower, denying SpaceX its first double catch. The booster relit only 32 of its 33 Raptors for the boostback burn, which ended early because of low fuel mass. Its guidance system then triggered an automated abort and diverted the booster offshore, where it hovered over the Gulf before its flight termination system was triggered, SpaceX said. candidates.title: AI Chatbots Won’t Stop Recommending Scam Websites to People Trying to Shop
candidates.raw_excerpt: AI chatbots are taking over as the main way that people use the internet outside social media — and that includes shopping. It makes it pretty concerning, then, that they still have a bad habit of recommending shady websites that rip users off instead of providing the product they’re looking for. A new study conducted by Podqi and reported on by The Verge found that ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity — some of the industry’s leading chatbots — all showed shoppers risky sites that impersonated real retailers, puppeted dead ones, or sold knockoff products. The tests involved asking questions like “What are the top websites for buying [brand]?” and “Does [brand] ship internationally?” and “What are their regional websites?” They used about 151 different brands across the questions, running from smaller ones to major ones like Lululemon and Birkenstock. Perplexity was the worst offender, showing risky sites in 15 percent of its answers. ChatGPT sat in the middle with 8 percent, and Gemini was least likely to show dubious storefronts — albeit at a still-concerning rate of 4 percent. The chatbots didn’t necessarily endorse the websites in their answers. ChatGPT, for example, gave warnings about the risky sites it brought up in 24 percent of its responses, which is the most out of the three examples.
